svg.text: FIG 03: HIGHER DERIVATIVES, INITIAL RATE OF CHANGE & STATE VARIABLE ARCHITECTURE
Initial Derivative Constraints • di_L/dt(0⁺) = v_L(0⁺)/L • dv_C/dt(0⁺) = i_C(0⁺)/C • Differentiated KVL/KCL for Second Derivatives

g.text: The Constitutive Rate Equations at t = 0⁺
Although inductor current i_L and capacitor voltage v_C are continuous at t = 0,
their first-order time derivatives CAN AND DO JUMP instantaneously!
Step 1: Determine Non-State Terminal Quantities at t = 0⁺
• Form the static resistive equivalent circuit at t = 0⁺.
• Dynamic elements are replaced by DC sources: L → I₀, C → V₀.
• Write KVL and KCL to solve for inductor voltage v_L(0⁺) and capacitor
Step 2: Divide by Dynamic Parameter (L or C)
Zero calculus required! Converted entirely into DC circuit analysis!
Solved Classroom Drill: Initial Slope in Series RLC
Unenergized series RLC circuit (R=10 Ω, L=2 H, C=0.5 F) connected to V_s = 100 V at t=0:
2. KVL around the loop at t = 0⁺:
3. First Derivative of Current at t = 0⁺:
4. First Derivative of Capacitor Voltage at t = 0⁺:
• Inductor voltage jumped from 0 V to 100 V instantly! It absorbs the ENTIRE source
voltage at t = 0⁺ because resistor has 0 V (i=0) and capacitor has 0 V (uncharged).
• Inductor current starts rising from zero with a steep initial slope of +50 A/s.
• Capacitor voltage starts rising from zero with a FLAT HORIZONTAL tangent
(slope = 0 V/s), because current feeding it starts from zero!
Exam Diagnostic: Curve v_C(t) leaves the origin tangentially to the horizontal axis!
At t = 0⁺, every energy storage element is strictly modeled by an equivalent source:
1. Inductor L with Initial Current I₀ = i_L(0⁻):
Replace with an Independent Current Source of value I₀.
(If I₀ = 0, current source of 0 A is an OPEN CIRCUIT).
2. Capacitor C with Initial Voltage V₀ = v_C(0⁻):
Replace with an Independent Voltage Source of value V₀.
(If V₀ = 0, voltage source of 0 V is a SHORT CIRCUIT).
Bridge circuit with switch closing at t=0 connecting DC 50 V to an R-L branch
in parallel with an R-C branch: R₁=10 Ω, L=2 H, R₂=20 Ω, C=100 μF (initially unenergized):
• Inductor branch: L becomes an OPEN CIRCUIT (i_L(0⁺) = 0 A).
• Capacitor branch: C becomes a SHORT CIRCUIT (v_C(0⁺) = 0 V).
Capacitor branch current: i₂(0⁺) = (50 V - 0 V) / 20 Ω = 2.5 A
In the previous circuit, observe the voltage across resistor R₂ (20 Ω):
After switching (t = 0⁺): v_{R2}(0⁺) = i₂(0⁺) · 20 Ω = 50 V !
Resistor voltage jumped instantly by 50 V! Resistor current jumped by 2.5 A!
Resistors have NO inertia and NO continuity obligation.
Only the capacitor voltage (v_C = 0 V) and inductor current (i_L = 0 A) stayed continuous.
1. L never allows its current to change: Model as Current Source.
2. C never allows its voltage to change: Model as Voltage Source.
3. Use standard KVL / KCL / Nodal / Mesh analysis on the resulting network.
4. Calculate unknown branch voltages across inductors and currents through capacitors.
Provides instantaneous access to all first-order rate derivatives!
The Differentiated KVL Algorithm for d²i/dt²
GATE frequently asks for higher derivatives at t = 0⁺:
1. Write the exact time-domain KVL or KCL equation for all t > 0.
2. Differentiate the entire equation once with respect to time t.
3. Take the temporal limit as t → 0⁺.
4. Substitute the previously evaluated initial values and first derivatives!
Complete Mathematical Derivation for Series RLC
Circuit: DC voltage V_s applied to series R-L-C at t = 0 with zero initial energy:
Step 1: KVL loop equation for t > 0:
Step 2: Differentiate with respect to t:
Since V_s is constant DC: d(V_s)/dt ≡ 0. And dv_C/dt = i(t) / C:
Since i(0⁺) = 0 and di/dt(0⁺) = V_s / L:
Using parameters from previous drill: V_s = 100 V, R = 10 Ω, L = 2 H, C = 0.5 F:
The negative second derivative indicates concavity downwards: as current rises,
its rate of growth is actively decelerating due to growing resistive drop iR!
Differentiating once more with respect to time:
Any higher derivative can be evaluated without ever solving the differential equation!
In modern network theory, circuits are modeled in standard first-order vector form:
ẋ(t) = A · x(t) + B · u(t) (State Equation)
• State variables are ALWAYS chosen as the INDEPENDENT capacitor voltages v_C(t)
and INDEPENDENT inductor currents i_L(t): x = [v_C1, v_C2, ..., i_L1, i_L2]ᵀ.
• The number of state variables equals the number of independent energy storage elements.
State Equations for Series RLC Circuit
Let state variables be x₁ = v_C(t) and x₂ = i_L(t). Input u(t) = V_s:
C · ẋ₁ = x₂ ⟹ ẋ₁ = 0 · x₁ + (1/C) · x₂ + 0 · u
L · ẋ₂ = u - x₁ - R · x₂ ⟹ ẋ₂ = (-1/L) · x₁ + (-R/L) · x₂ + (1/L) · u
The natural frequencies (poles) of the network are the eigenvalues of matrix A:
Matches the classical second-order characteristic equation identically!
• Trace of A = sum of eigenvalues: Tr(A) = s₁ + s₂ = -R/L = -2α.
• Determinant of A = product of eigenvalues: det(A) = s₁ · s₂ = 1/(LC) = ω₀².
Summary: Initial Values vs. Higher Derivatives
Exam Rule: Never differentiate before finding static model values at 0⁺!
